analysis.one_liner: Weakens the consumer finance watchdog's funding, enforcement powers, and direct oversight of banks and lenders.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee advanced the bill 28-21 on a party-line vote in September 2026; no floor vote has happened yet.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill rewrites the rules for the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, the federal agency that polices credit cards, mortgages, debt collectors, and payday-style loans. It would end the Bureau's independent funding and force it to compete for money through the annual congressional spending process. It would also narrow the standards the Bureau can use to crack down on harmful practices, let banks above a much higher asset size escape direct Bureau supervision, shield bank-offered small-dollar loans from most liability, and take debt-collection lawsuits out of the Bureau's reach. A separate section sets federal rules for paycheck-advance apps and stops states from regulating those apps as lenders.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks and credit unions that would escape direct Bureau supervision, lenders offering small-dollar loans, debt-collection law firms, insurers, and paycheck-advance apps all gain from reduced oversight or new legal protections.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the asset threshold at which banks, savings associations, and credit unions face direct Bureau supervision from $10 billion to $30 billion, adjusts it upward automatically for economic growth, and lets covered institutions elect to be supervised by their banking regulator instead of the Bureau.

Creates a safe harbor for insured banks and credit unions (and their third-party partners) offering loans or credit lines of $3,500 or less, shielding compliant products from federal civil penalties and private damages claims under the Truth in Lending Act.
Excludes licensed attorneys and law firms engaged in litigation to collect a debt from the legal definition of 'debt collector,' removing them from Bureau oversight of debt-collection litigation.

Lets a company avoid monetary penalties if it made a 'good-faith effort to comply' with the ban on unfair, deceptive, or abusive practices, presumes injuries were 'reasonably avoidable' when conduct was disclosed, and gives companies a 180-day window to cure problems before the Bureau can sue.

Blocks the Bureau from bringing enforcement actions against persons regulated by a state insurance regulator for their insurance business, and forbids the Bureau from treating discriminatory practices as 'unfair, deceptive, or abusive.'

Caps penalties by barring the Bureau from seeking civil money penalties for conduct occurring before the most recent consumer-compliance exam rating, limits the Bureau's market-monitoring functions, and restricts state enforcement powers.

Establishes federal rules for earned wage access apps — requiring a no-cost option, disclosure of fees and tips, and dispute processes — while barring states from treating complying services as credit or loans.

analysis.who_pays: Consumers who rely on the Bureau's enforcement against predatory lending, wrongful fees, and abusive debt collection; refunds and penalties recovered from violators would shrink, and money left over in the civil penalty fund would go to the Treasury instead of victims.
analysis.who_pays_short: Consumers with complaints about lenders and collectors

drawbacks.text: Subjecting the Bureau to annual appropriations makes its budget dependent on each year's spending fights, unlike its current funding stream from the Federal Reserve, which supporters of the bill argue is unaccountable but critics say invites political starvation of enforcement.

Narrowing the 'abusive' standard, requiring concrete and quantifiable injury, adding a good-faith defense, and presuming that disclosed terms were 'reasonably avoidable' would make it much harder for the Bureau to win cases against practices that harm consumers in aggregate even when fine print was disclosed.

Raising the supervision threshold to $30 billion removes dozens of midsize banks and credit unions from direct Bureau examination, leaving their consumer-law compliance to their prudential regulators.

The bill's supporters argue it adds needed accountability: cost-benefit analysis for rules, mandatory OMB reviews of major regulations, an independent Inspector General for the Bureau, and definitions of vague standards, plus a safe harbor that could encourage banks to offer cheaper installment credit than high-cost payday loans.
A neutral element: the bill orders a government study of buy now pay later services rather than regulating them now.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's transparency and Inspector General provisions have some merit, but its core effect is to sharply reduce the main federal watchdog's ability to investigate, sue, and collect from financial firms — the accountability gains are procedural while the enforcement losses are substantive. The safe harbor for small-dollar bank loans is the strongest consumer argument, but it is paired with broad carve-outs for debt collectors, insurers, and midsize banks that cut the other way.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared a committee vote 28-21 on September 16, 2026, but has not yet come up for a vote on the House floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Andy Barr introduced the bill on August 31, 2026, with 30 Republican cosponsors; all cosponsors are Republicans.
It was referred to four committees — Financial Services, Judiciary, Small Business, and Oversight and Government Reform — for consideration of the provisions in each one's jurisdiction.
On September 16, 2026, the Financial Services Committee held a markup and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 28 to 21.
No floor vote has occurred, and the current Congress ends on January 3, 2027.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, the financial industry and the bill's sponsors, who got a favorable committee vote; consumers are unaffected until the bill reaches the floor and would only be affected if it becomes law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Bill supporters and the financial industry

sides.party_line_note: All 30 cosponsors are Republicans, and the 28-21 committee vote in September 2026 split along party lines; no Democrat has signed on.

industries.industry: Midsize and large banks and credit unions
industries.note: Direct Bureau supervision would now start at $30 billion in assets instead of $10 billion, with automatic inflation-style increases, and qualifying institutions could elect their banking regulator instead. Fewer institutions would face the Bureau's examiners for consumer-law compliance.

A Truth in Lending Act safe harbor for loans up to $3,500 through insured banks, credit unions, and their partners shields compliant products from federal penalties and private damages suits, reducing legal risk for high-cost credit programs.

Attorneys and law firms suing to collect debts would be excluded from the 'debt collector' definition, removing Bureau oversight of debt-collection litigation — the segment where consumers most often complain about false filings and robo-signed lawsuits.

The bill legitimizes paycheck-advance apps as a non-credit product under federal law and preempts states from treating them as loans, locking in their fee-and-tip model, but in exchange requires a no-cost option, fee disclosures, and dispute processes.

The Bureau's enforcement against people regulated by state insurance regulators would be sharply narrowed, leaving state insurance regulation as the primary check on insurance-related financial products.

analysis.trajectory: With a favorable committee vote and a House Republican majority, the likely next step is a House floor vote, where similar Bureau-restructuring bills have previously passed. The Senate, where Republicans hold 53 of 100 seats, has historically not acted on House bills of this kind, and the session ends January 3, 2027, leaving a short window.
